claims.text: The proposed alloy has the composition W70Ta10Mo10Re10 in atomic percent.
The proposed alloy is a refractory high-entropy alloy.
The proposed alloy can serve as a low-activation structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components in fusion reactors.
The proposed alloy has enhanced irradiation resistance.
The proposed alloy has enhanced high-temperature mechanical properties.
The alloy will be fabricated by powder metallurgy.
The fabricated alloy will have a polycrystalline microstructure with an average grain size of 10 μm.
The fabricated alloy will reach 95% of its theoretical density.
Adjusting Ta, Mo, and Re concentrations can balance irradiation resistance against high-temperature mechanical properties.
Ta, Mo, and Re are low-activation elements in the stated fusion-material context.
The relevant fusion-reactor environment can reach 1000°C, neutron fluxes of 10^14 n/cm²s, and plasma-exposure durations of 1000 hours.
Ta and Mo segregate to grain boundaries in the proposed alloy.
Grain-boundary segregation of Ta and Mo reduces radiation-induced defect formation and thereby enhances irradiation resistance.
Grain-boundary segregation of Ta and Mo inhibits grain-boundary sliding and thereby improves high-temperature mechanical properties.
The optimized composition increases grain-boundary cohesion.
The optimized composition reduces impurity diffusion.
Relative to traditional fusion-reactor materials, the optimized alloy will provide a 20% increase in irradiation resistance as measured in dpa.
Relative to traditional fusion-reactor materials, the optimized alloy will provide a 15% increase in high-temperature mechanical properties as measured in MPa.
The hypothesis is falsified if the alloy shows both less than a 15% irradiation-resistance increase and less than a 10% high-temperature mechanical-property increase under matched conditions.
